newsitem.title: USA: Clinton awards medal to astronaut Shannon Lucid.
newsitem.headline: Clinton awards medal to astronaut Shannon Lucid.

text.p: President Bill Clinton honoured astronaut Shannon Lucid on Monday, saying her record-breaking 188 days in space were an inspiration to women and a shining example of U.S.-Russian cooperation.

Lucid became the 10th recipient of the Congressional Space Medal of Honour, and the first woman to receive the award, for her mission this year during which she spent more than six months orbiting Earth with two Russians in cramped, uncomfortable conditions aboard the Russian space station Mir.

In an Oval Office ceremony, Clinton hailed Lucid as a national hero for her mission -- the longest by any American and any woman of any nation -- and an inspiration to all Americans, but especially to women.

"Most pioneers set their sights on just one frontier. Shannon Lucid has pushed to the furthermost reaches of two -- the frontiers of both space and science," said Clinton, who was suffering from hoarseness.

"She has done so with brainpower, willpower, courage, skill and good humour," he said. "She has exceeded a universe of expectation. Perhaps even more than she knows, she has set a remarkable example for a new generation of young Americans, especially young women."
Clinton said the mission also cemented U.S. cooperation in space with Russia and demonstrated that joint space exploration could deepen the friendship between the two former enemies.
In her remarks, Lucid took up this theme, saying she and her two Russian colleagues had discussed how all three had grown up fearing each other's country as Cold War rivals.
"What the flight really was, was a story of two great spacefaring nations that cooperated together, that worked together and it was just a foretaste of what could happen in the future," she said.

In television interviews, Lucid said she had emerged from the mission in surprisingly good shape, demonstrating the feasibility of long space flights. "There was some calcium loss in the bones. But I had very good bones to start with, so my bones are still in very, very good shape and everybody was very happy," she said.
Her blood chemistry showed no significant changes. "There was nothing outside of the normal range in my blood when I got back as compared to pre-flight," she said.
Her medal citation stated Lucid's contributions "are an inspiration to all who have gazed into the nighttime sky."

Previous recipients of the medal include Alan Shepard, the first American in orbit, John Glenn, now an Ohio senator who was present at the ceremony, and Neil Armstrong, the first man to step on the moon.
